title: Motivation and Emotion
summary: Motives, wants, needs, interests and desires direct us towards chosen goals. Motivation pushes us to reach goals; it needs an optimum level of arousal (too little makes us dull, too much makes us withdraw); it is influenced by pleasing properties of external stimuli (money, grades, food) and by thoughts and expectations. Intrinsic motivation comes from within (personal enjoyment); extrinsic motivation is based on external rewards (money, grades). Needs are ordered: basic needs are met first.

Abraham Maslow: biological (primary) needs at the base, then safety, belongingness and love, self-esteem, cognitive needs (knowledge, understanding), aesthetic needs (order and beauty) and finally self-actualisation (full potential: self-aware, socially responsive, open to challenges). A person may move up and down the hierarchy; it may not hold true in all cultures (in Sweden and Norway quality of life and social needs are valued over self-actualisation; in some cultures job security matters more than job satisfaction).

Primary needs are biological: hunger, thirst, oxygen, rest, sleep, temperature regulation, shelter, excretion and sex; they must be met for survival and some (hunger, sleep) are cyclical. Homeostasis is the body's state of balance (water, temperature, glucose). Hunger is signalled by stomach contractions (hunger pangs) and low blood glucose and protein; smell, taste and look of food add to it. Thirst results from loss of water by perspiration, breathing and urination. Environmental influences on hunger: learned liking and habits, stress, external cues (dinner time), dietary restraints.

Secondary (psychological or social) needs are learnt in social groups, particularly the family: achievement (strive for success and excellence), affiliation (seek company, make friends), power (influence and control others), nurturance (care for others, as Mother Teresa), aggression and exploration (seek novelty). Their strength differs among persons (Nelson Mandela's commitment to difficult goals). Needs are also classed as existence needs, relatedness needs and growth needs.

Emotions are strong feelings associated with pleasant or unpleasant experiences. Functions: they prepare us for action (fear makes us run), help arrange activities and future behaviour (positive emotions act as reinforcement), and help us interact effectively with others. Components: (1) physiological changes – heart rate, blood pressure, pupil size, perspiration, faster breathing, dry mouth; (2) behavioural changes and emotional expression – facial expression, posture, gestures; six primary emotions in facial expressions: fear, anger, sadness, surprise, disgust and happiness, recognised worldwide; (3) emotional feelings – personal labelling of the feeling shaped by past experience and culture. Cognition (understanding of the situation) is important: sometimes we think then feel, sometimes act first. We often feel a mixture of emotions.

The six basic emotions are expressed universally, but display rules differ by culture (Japanese show less emotional display than Italians); display rules are learnt in childhood. 'Masking' of emotion is a pasted-on smile on getting an unwanted gift.

Both are forces that move, activate, control and plan behaviour. The feeling part of emotion has a motivational component, helping us get what we want and avoid what we do not want. Emotions can serve as motives (a frightened child cries for comfort). Satisfying primary and secondary needs brings satisfaction, joy and pride.

sa: Motivation pushes us to goals and needs optimum arousal; it is influenced by pleasing external stimuli such as money and food; it results from thoughts and expectations and may be intrinsic or extrinsic; and needs are ordered, basic needs first.
Describe the factors in the hunger need.
Stomach contractions and low blood glucose and protein cause hunger; smell, taste and look of food add to it; environment matters through learned liking, stress, external cues and dietary restraints.
Social motives are learned in groups, mainly the family: achievement, affiliation, power, nurturance, aggression and exploration; their strength differs from person to person.
Emotions prepare us for action, help arrange activities and future behaviour (positive emotions reinforce), and help us interact effectively with others by showing how we are likely to act.
Explain the components of emotion with an example.
Physiological changes (heart rate, perspiration before an exam), behavioural expression (facial expressions, gestures) and subjective feelings labelled by experience and culture.
The six basic emotions are expressed universally, but cultures differ in display rules learnt through childhood experiences; people may also mask emotions, as with a polite smile at an unwanted gift.
la: Maslow ranked needs from biological at the base, then safety, belongingness and love, self-esteem, cognitive needs, aesthetic needs, and self-actualisation at the top. Lower needs are met first, but a person may move up and down the hierarchy and cultures differ (Sweden and Norway value social needs; some cultures value job security over satisfaction).
Discuss primary and secondary needs with examples and environmental influences.

Primary needs (hunger, thirst, oxygen, sleep, warmth) arise from physiological imbalance and homeostasis; hunger is influenced by learned liking, stress, external cues and dietary restraints. Secondary needs (achievement, affiliation, power, nurturance, aggression, exploration) are learned socially, e.g. Mother Teresa high on nurturance and Mandela on achievement.
What are emotions? Explain their functions and components.

Emotions are strong feelings from pleasant or unpleasant experiences. They prepare us for action, organise future behaviour, and help interaction. Components: physiological changes, behavioural expression (six primary facial emotions) and feelings; cognition is essential, and culture shapes display rules.
Discuss the role of motivation and emotion in organising behaviour.

Both activate, control and plan behaviour. Motivation is accompanied by emotions (success brings joy and pride) and emotions motivate us to repeat or avoid situations. Emotions can serve as motives (a frightened child seeks comfort); without them we would act in a robotic fashion.
